Good study selection criteria 2. Direct measurements of hypertrophy 3. It is a systematic review so high in the hierachy of evidence pyramid Weaknesses: 1. Small number of studies included 2. Lack of standardisation between studies 3. No nutritional control Mechanical Tension This is the mechanism that is proposed to be the main cause of hypertrophy. It does by leading to signal transduction and in increasing MPS Volume Training There is evidence to suggest dose-response relationship between volume and an increase in MPS. In recent years, volume has received a lot of attention. Some studies have proposed a dose-response relationship, some have proposed an inverted "U" shape. Study Design Studies were chosen with the following criteria: 1. They were randomised controlled trials comparing different number of sets with the same load assignment 2. Studies lasted for a minimum of 6 weeks 3. Participants were 18-35 years old 4. Studies reported direct measuring of thickenss or CSA 5. Studies were peer-reviewed and published in journals Two independent observers reviewed the studied and concluded whether they were appropriate to include. When disagreement was present, a third observer was asked. Included studies Seven studies met the criteria where low volume groups were included with moderate and high volume groups. Six were included as these had participants perming more than 12 weekly sets Low volume groups were excluded from the quantitative analysis Volume Criteria Low Volume (LV): < 12 sets Moderate Volume (MV): 12-20 sets High Volume (HV): > 20 sets Research Page 2

High Volume (HV): > 20 sets Muscles Tested The Quadriceps femoris, biceps brachii and triceps brachii were measured Findings There was a favourable trend towards HV training but there were no differences beween MV nad HV training for the quadriceps femoris and biceps brachii. HV seemed to induce greater muscle size increases in the triceps brachii. The training frequencies differed between studies. HV training may optimally be used when distributed to a greater frequency. Previous training volume of participants may have been relevant. One reason why the triceps brachii may have shown a favourable tendency to HV training is due to the lack of measurements in the triceps brachii. It could also be explained than the growth of the triceps brachii is not uniform and multi-joint exercise affect the lateral-head and single-joint ones can affect the long-head more. Limitations 1. The number of studies included is small 2. There is no standardisation between moderate and high volumes 3. Quadriceps femoris measurements were not consistent, measurements of different areas were included and have been used for comparison 4. Caloric intake and supplement was not reported for most of the studies Conclusions The optimum training volume range lies within 12-20 weekly sets per week . Increasing frequency can allow for more volume to be successfully performed. Multi-joint exercises counted for the triceps brachii volume and so 12-20 weekly sets may be optimal rather than HV. 4 Loading Recommendations for Muscle Strength, Hypertrophy, and Local Endurance: A Re-Examination of the Repetition Continuum 08 November 2025 13:18 Title: Loading Recommendations for Muscle Strength, Hypertrophy, and Local Endurance: A Re- Examination of the Repetition Continuum Authors: Brad Schoenfeld, Jozo Grgic, Derrick Van Every, Daniel Plotkin Link: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7927075/ Strengths: 1. Comprehensive review of literaure up to 2021 2. Challenges a traditional training protocol 3. Gives practical applications Weaknesses 1. Narrative reviews may present bias in study selection Repetition Continuum (RC) The theory that the number of repetitions performed at a given load will result in specific adaptations. It is believed that heavy-load training results in strength adaptation, moderate-loads result in hypertrophy and low-load training result in endurance. Current research fails to support the presumptations that are made to allow this theory to be true as claimed by authors. RC load recommendations Strength is Low repetitions with heavy loads (1-5 reps with 80%-100% of 1RM) Hypertrophy is Moderate repetitions with moderate loads (8-12 reps with 60%-80% of 1RM) Endurance is high repetitions with light loads (15+ repetitions with loads below 60% of 1RM) RC hypertrophy zone Typically the 8-12 rep range has been labelled as a "hypertrophy zone" due to the belief that moderate loads are optimal for muscle growth. This has been used in guidelines such as ACSM RT Guidelines. Support for RC Hypertrophy Acute studies have shown greater post-exercise elevations in anabolic hormones when training in zone moderate loads but the relevance of these hormonal spice on adaptation is unclear. Criticism of support Some studies have shown that low-load training shows an acute impared MPS response while other studies show increases in mixed and myofibrillar protein synthesis. Level of effort (LoE) is stated to be an explanation for the variation in results. Studies that show an impaired anabolic response with low-load training employed protocals where participants stopped well short of fatigue. However, LoE is essential for maximizing hypertrophy adaptation in load-load training. Studies that included a high LoE with low-loads showed that the MPS response was at least as robust as high-load training. Early evidence showed that light-load training produced suboptimal hypertrophy. Wernbom (2007) concluded a hypertrophy benefit with loads >60% 1RM. However multiple studies have since then been published on this matter and a meta analysis by Schoenfeld et al. found no differences in hypertrophy between studies comparing high to low loads. Morton et al. found that training with 8-12 RM compared to 20-25RM produced signicant changed in LBM and type I and II fiber CSA of the vastus lateralus in trained individuals following a 12-week full- body program with no observable differences between groups. On a set-equated basis, low-load sets would result in greater volume loads compared to low-load due to the higher reptitions performed Few studies have investigated high vs load-loads with equated volumes. Lopes et al. found no differences in FFM between volume-equated groups of low (3 sets of 20RM) and high (6 sets of 10RM) loads. Fiber specific training Some researchers have proposed that training across rep-ranges may induce fiber-type specific response where low-loads promote hypertrophy of type I fibers and heavy-loads promote hypertrophy of type II fibers. Low-loads may help in hypertrophy of type I fibers by increasing time-under-tension (due to type I fibers being "endurance-oriented") as well as increased acidosis and accumulation of H+ during high- rep training may interfere with calcium binding in type II fibers and therefore placing a greater burden on type I fibers to maintain force output. However, results from acute and longitudinal research comparing fiber type-specific hypertrophy in high and load-load training groups have been mixed. These findings cast doubt to a load-induced effect on fiber type however the study didn't assess fiber growth with muscle biopsy. A meta-analysis included studies that performed muscle biopsy and compared the effect of low vs high load training on type I and II muscle fiber CSA when training to muscle failure. The analysis found no significant difference between load and high loads. Low-Threshold for hypetrophy 30% 1RM has shown to be the low threshold for hypertrophy as it has shown to give comparible results to heavier loads. Overall Conclusion There is no clear hypertrophy zone and hypertrophy can be achiebved between a wide spectrum of ranges >= 30% 1RM. Focuses on programming more than hypertrophy which is a smaller part of my dissertation Definitions Hypertrophy training - Training that directly causes muscle growth (or maintenance in hypocaloric conditions) or improves systems underlying muscle growth Repetion - single executionof an exercise from the desired starting point through the terminal range of motion and back to starting point 1RM - One repetition maximum; the heaviest weight a person can lift for one repetition Set - a collection of continuous repetitions of an exercises seperated by bouts of rest Microcycle - shortest training cycle that includes session and rest days repeated. Mesocycle - an organised sequence of microcycles that elicit a set of distinct adaptations. Typically involving an accumalation and a deload phase Accumulation phase - a series of sequential microcycles within a mesocycle where training gets progressively more challenging via a combination of sets, reps, load or relative effort increases. Deload phase - an entire microcycle composed of lower volume, load, relative effort sessions with the purpose of reducing fatigue while preserving adaptations Block - A block of training is one or more mesocycles that share a specific goal such as muscle gain or fat loss Macrocycle - A sequence of training blocks used to enhance longitudinal performance gains. Periodisation - The logical sequencing of training variables for the purpose of eliciting maximal adaptations, reducing injury rates, and peaking an athlete for best performance Autoregulation - Altering training variables based on needs Volume - Sets per session or sets per week Research Page 18
